original_question: For which separable Banach spaces X does the Lebesgue-Bochner space L_1([0, 1], X) contain a subspace isomorphic to ℓ_2(X)?
target_in_paper: Problem 5.6 (Diestel) in §5.2, Structural properties: “For which separable Banach spaces X the space L_1([0,1], X) contains a copy of ℓ_2(X)?”
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper’s target almost verbatim: it asks about separable Banach spaces X, the specific Lebesgue-Bochner space L_1([0,1],X), and whether it contains ℓ_2(X) as an isomorphic subspace.
missing_details: The paper’s official wording is “contains a copy of ℓ_2(X)”; by the notation section this is equivalent to “contains a closed linear subspace isomorphic to ℓ_2(X)”.
The paper works throughout with real Banach spaces.
[0,1] is equipped with Lebesgue measure, so L_1([0,1],X) means the Lebesgue-Bochner space of equivalence classes of strongly measurable functions f:[0,1]→X with ∫_0^1 ||f(t)|| dt < ∞.
To make the question fully stand-alone, ℓ_2(X) should be identified as the ℓ_2-direct sum of countably many copies of X.
The scope should remain exactly “separable Banach spaces X”; it should not be broadened to arbitrary Banach spaces or to general L_1(μ,X) spaces.
refined_question: Over the real scalars, for which separable Banach spaces X does the Lebesgue-Bochner space L_1([0,1],X)—that is, the space of equivalence classes of strongly measurable functions f:[0,1]→X with ∫_0^1 ||f(t)|| dt < ∞, where [0,1] carries Lebesgue measure—contain a copy of ℓ_2(X), the ℓ_2-direct sum of countably many copies of X?
equivalent_formulation: Equivalently, for which separable real Banach spaces X does L_1([0,1],X) contain a closed linear subspace isomorphic to ℓ_2(X)?
justification: This is exactly Problem 5.6 in §5.2. The surrounding discussion distinguishes it from the neighboring Problem 5.5 about whether ℓ_2(X) and L_2([0,1],X) are isomorphic, and it notes that although ℓ_2 embeds into L_1[0,1], a universal positive answer for ℓ_2(X) fails in general; the paper gives X=ℓ_1 as an example. The notation section also makes your phrase “subspace isomorphic to” formally equivalent to the paper’s “contains a copy of.”
